predictions.title: Frontier-class open-weight LLM runs single-node under 256GB by Q4 2026
predictions.body: A frontier-class open-weight model (a release benchmarking near the closed-source frontier on coding and reasoning, in the GLM-5.2 / 700B-plus mixture-of-experts class) will be demonstrably runnable on a single high-memory workstation node holding 256GB or less of combined memory by the end of Q4 2026, via aggressive sub-2-bit selective-precision quantization, with a published reproducible recipe and quality measured on a public benchmark rather than vendor self-report. Unsloth's Dynamic GGUF builds already squeezed Z.ai's 744B GLM-5.2 from a 1.51TB checkpoint to roughly 217-239GB, but those compression and quality numbers are Unsloth's own and unverified, and 1-2 bit quantization at this aggression trades measurable accuracy for memory. The prediction lands when at least one such recipe is independently reproduced and its accuracy retention published, confirming that the heaviest open-weight tier has crossed from multi-GPU-cluster territory into single-node, on-prem reach. This sharpens the standing split: advanced or peak-quality work still routes to cloud APIs, while daily and privacy-sensitive workloads can increasingly run locally on owned hardware.

reasoning.because: Unsloth shrank a 1.51TB 744B GLM-5.2 to ~217-239GB via selective sub-2-bit quantization.
reasoning.given: Selective-precision quant keeps cutting open-weight memory faster than model size grows.
reasoning.so_that: Teams self-host a near-frontier model on owned single-node hardware for daily, privacy-sensitive work.
reasoning.landing: Reproduced sub-256GB single-node run, accuracy published, by Q4 2026.
reasoning.plain_language: By late 2026 one of the biggest top-tier open AI models will run on a single powerful computer, not a server farm.

predictions.summary: Unsloth squeezed Z.ai's 744B GLM-5.2 from 1.51TB to roughly 217-239GB via sub-2-bit selective-precision quantization. By Q4 2026 a frontier-class open-weight model will run single-node under 256GB with a reproduced recipe and published accuracy, putting the heaviest open models within on-prem reach.

predictions.title: OpenClaw ships default-deny tool and network gating out-of-box by Q4 2026
predictions.body: A named open coding-agent harness ships least-privilege execution as the shipped out-of-box default rather than an opt-in flag by Q4 2026. The most probable first mover is OpenClaw: its June 2026.6.x releases already patched concrete injection paths, tightened Docker sandbox boundaries, added Browser CDP endpoint validation, pinned SSH tunnel checks to loopback, and began rejecting unsafe tool, package, and response lengths. The prediction calls for the next step: a fresh stable release whose default profile denies tool calls, outbound network access, and MCP credential exposure unless an operator explicitly grants them, so that a clean install runs sandboxed-and-gated with no extra configuration. NVIDIA's NemoClaw (stricter network-policy defaults around OpenShell sandboxes) and Nous Research's Hermes Agent (MCP credential filtering, SSRF protection, and a Tirith pre-execution scan) are the same-direction alternatives that could land first. The catalyst is the converging security evidence: OWASP's 2026 agentic report ties nearly every risk category to real CVEs and ranks Claude Code among the most advisory-laden coding-agent repos, while StakeBench found no tested agent configuration resists prompt injection (41-68% indirect, above 79% direct). When the model layer cannot be made robust, the harness layer carries the defense, and least-privilege only works as a default. Verification: a tagged release or its changelog/docs stating that capability, network, or MCP-credential gating is enabled by default on a fresh install, not behind an opt-in setting.

reasoning.because: OpenClaw 2026.6.x already hardened sandbox, CDP, SSH, and length limits, but gating stays opt-in.
reasoning.given: StakeBench shows no agent config resists prompt injection, so defense must move to the harness.
reasoning.so_that: a clean install of a named harness runs sandboxed and capability-gated with zero extra operator configuration.
reasoning.landing: A named coding-agent harness defaults to capability gating by Q4 2026.
reasoning.plain_language: A popular coding robot will block its own risky actions by default, so you stay safe without changing any settings.

predictions.summary: An open coding-agent harness, likely OpenClaw, is predicted to ship least-privilege execution as the out-of-box default by Q4 2026, gating tool calls, network access, and MCP credentials unless granted. The driver is evidence no agent setup resists prompt injection, moving defense to the harness.

predictions.title: AI-agent procurement adds a numeric prompt-injection-resistance bar by Q2 2027
predictions.body: A standards body, regulator, or large enterprise/government buyer will name a quantified prompt-injection-resistance score as a stated, pass/fail requirement in an agentic-AI procurement gate, framework control, or certification. The trigger is the shift this cycle from hypothetical to measured: OWASP's State of Agentic AI Security and Governance v2.01 now ties nearly every agentic-risk category to concrete CVEs, vendor advisories, and breach reports, ranking the repositories carrying the most advisories (n8n 57, Claude Code 22, AutoGPT 15, Dify 13, Roo-Code 11) and mapping prompt injection to six of its ten Top 10 categories. In parallel, the StakeBench benchmark (Nanyang Technological University, ST Engineering, IBM Research, and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) ran 3,168 adversarial trials and found indirect-injection success of 41.67%-68.16% and direct attacks above 79% across every tested configuration, with none landing in the robust-behavior region. Once an attack class has both a documented incident trail and a published benchmark with numeric pass thresholds, buyers stop accepting vendor self-attestation and start writing a measurable bar into contracts. Expect the first such gate to cite a named benchmark or a numeric maximum injection-success rate rather than asking vendors to 'mitigate prompt injection' in prose. This makes resistance an auditable acceptance criterion, not a best-effort claim, and gives the OWASP/StakeBench numbers a downstream consumer.

reasoning.because: OWASP v2.01 now ties agentic risk to real CVEs and StakeBench's 3,168 trials found no robust config
reasoning.given: an attack class with an incident trail plus a numeric benchmark outgrows vendor-prose mitigation
reasoning.so_that: a buyer or framework writes a numeric injection-resistance bar into a gate, replacing self-attestation with an audit
reasoning.landing: First named numeric injection-resistance procurement gate appears by Q2 2027
reasoning.plain_language: Buyers will start demanding AI agents pass a real score for resisting tricky inputs, not just promise they handle them.

predictions.summary: OWASP's 2026 report ties agentic risks to real CVEs, and StakeBench found no agent configuration resists prompt injection. With an incident trail and a numeric benchmark in hand, a standards body or major buyer will write a quantified injection-resistance threshold into a procurement gate by Q2 2027.
